jaunt

JAWNT · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Jaunt is a short trip or excursion taken for pleasure.

Every Sunday, my grandfather took a leisurely jaunt down to the pier, just to watch the fishing boats come in.

Example

After finishing exams early, the roommates decided on an impromptu jaunt to the amusement park two towns over.

A jaunt is a short trip taken purely for enjoyment, usually without much planning -- here, a spur-of-the-moment visit to an amusement park.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

excursion: An excursion is a pleasure trip that is usually planned ahead — an organized event with a set destination, like a class excursion to a museum. A jaunt is looser and more spur-of-the-moment: you slip out on a jaunt without an itinerary, a sign-up sheet, or much of a plan at all.

outing: An outing is also a short trip taken for fun, but the word leans toward company — a family outing, a class outing, an event shared with a group. A jaunt can be entirely your own: one person slipping off for a quick, carefree trip is a jaunt, no group required.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

expedition: a long, carefully planned journey, often for a serious purpose

ordeal: a difficult and painful experience, the opposite of a fun trip

Where it sits · how long and demanding the outing is

stroll → jaunt → trek

stroll vs. jaunt: A stroll is just a short, leisurely walk, far more modest than an actual trip like a jaunt.

trek vs. jaunt: A trek is a long, arduous journey, a much bigger undertaking than a casual jaunt.

Build the Word

The pieces

root (uncertain origin) — jaunt: possibly related to the obsolete word 'jaunce,' meaning to jolt or trot a horse back and forth -- etymologists aren't fully certain of the connection (uncertain, possibly Middle French)

Put it together: Jaunt's origin is genuinely uncertain. Some word historians connect it to the obsolete English word jaunce, meaning to jolt or trot a horse back and forth tiringly -- ironic, since a modern jaunt is supposed to be easy and fun, not exhausting.

Use the root in a new word: junket: The reporters were invited on an all-expenses-paid junket to the film festival. (Junket isn't related to jaunt by root, but it describes a similar idea -- a pleasure trip, sometimes at someone else's expense.)
